chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.text:
Abstract
Short-form video is now a primary channel for news, advice, and commerce, yet viewers rarely have a fast way to judge
whether a clip is credible. This write-up documents CrediClip , a multi-platform system that accepts a
public TikTok, Instagram, or YouTube Shorts URL and returns a 0 to 100 credibility score, risk flags for misinformation,
scams, manipulation, and uncertainty, claim-level notes, and an explicit evidence-coverage breakdown. The system separates
a lightweight control plane on @Fly.io
from heavy media workers on @Oracle Cloud
that perform browser rendering, OCR, and speech recognition. A deterministic scoring engine combines six signals and,
critically, shrinks its output toward a neutral anchor when evidence is thin. Large language models are used only for
gated claim assessment, never for the final number. Across a 780-link YouTube batch the system completed every job
while correctly refusing to be confident on 97% of low-evidence inputs, and a worker-backed redesign for Instagram raised
average extracted evidence from 1 token to 131 tokens per video. I discuss the design decisions, the failed benchmark
gates that forced them, and the limitations that remain.
Keywords: credibility assessment, misinformation, short-form video, multimodal evidence extraction, OCR, ASR, LLM gating, trust and safety, explainable scoring, product management

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 1. Introduction
chunks.text:
1. Introduction
A 30-second clip can travel to millions of people before anyone checks its source. Research on social platforms has shown
that false stories spread farther, faster, and deeper than true ones, largely because novelty and emotional charge drive
sharing [1] . Short-form video amplifies that dynamic: the format is fast,
the context is minimal, and the persuasive layer (music, captions, a confident face) does a lot of work that text alone cannot.
I framed the problem around four failure modes a viewer faces, which later became the system's risk dimensions:
Misinformation: false or distorted claims spread before anyone can verify the source or context.
Scams: deceptive intent hidden behind polished content, fake offers, and manufactured urgency.
Manipulation: emotional pressure or synthetic media used to bypass critical thinking.
Uncertainty: unclear origin and weak context that leave viewers without trustworthy signals.
Figure 1. The four problem dimensions that shaped CrediClip's risk model.
The project was guided by three research questions:
RQ1. Can a single link-only workflow recover enough evidence (captions, transcripts, on-screen text, speech) from three very different platforms to support a credibility judgment?
RQ2. Can credibility be scored in a way that is explainable and reproducible , rather than delegated to a black-box model?

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 2. Background & related work
chunks.text:
2. Background & related work
CrediClip sits at the intersection of three research areas, each with a well-known benchmark that informed the design.

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 2.1 Claim verification
chunks.text:
2.1 Claim verification
FEVER framed fact checking as retrieving evidence and classifying a claim as Supported ,
Refuted , or Not Enough Info [2] . CrediClip adopts the same
three-way label set ( supported , refuted , not_enough_evidence ). The third label is
the most important one for this domain, because most short-form clips do not contain enough verifiable text to settle a claim.

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 2.2 Synthetic and manipulated media
chunks.text:
2.2 Synthetic and manipulated media
FaceForensics++ [3] and the
DeepFake Detection Challenge (DFDC) [4] established visual
benchmarks for manipulated faces, and ASVspoof [5] did the same
for spoofed and synthetic speech. These datasets define the reference frame for the manipulation and generation-origin signals.
In this MVP, manipulation is scored from textual and disclosure cues plus an optional
@AI or Not API hook; formal
evaluation against these visual and audio benchmarks is listed as future work (Section 13).

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 2.3 Speech and text extraction
chunks.text:
2.3 Speech and text extraction
Two open-source components made link-only analysis feasible: OpenAI's Whisper family for robust speech
recognition [6] , used here through the
@faster-whisper
implementation, and Tesseract for OCR of on-screen text [7] .
On-screen captions are often where short-form creators put their actual claims, so OCR is not a nice-to-have; it is a primary evidence channel.

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 3. Product framing
chunks.text:
3. Product framing
I approached CrediClip as a product owner first and a builder second. Before writing code, I defined who the user is, what
job they are hiring the product to do, and what a minimum credible output looks like.

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 3.1 Users and jobs to be done
chunks.text:
3.1 Users and jobs to be done
Everyday viewers who want a quick "should I trust this?" signal before sharing.
Moderators and trust-and-safety teams who need to triage large volumes of video with evidence attached.
Fact-checkers and researchers who need a fast first pass to decide what deserves human review.

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 3.2 Product principles
chunks.text:
3.2 Product principles
Link in, evidence out. The only required input is a URL. Caption and transcript fields are optional accelerators.
Explain every number. Each score ships with the signals, flags, and evidence counts that produced it.
Never fake certainty. When the system cannot see enough, the score says so by staying near neutral.
Keep the score deterministic. The same evidence should always produce the same score, which makes the system auditable.

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 3.3 The user flow
chunks.text:
3.3 The user flow
Paste a link. The user submits any public short-form video URL.
Detect the platform. The system identifies Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube Shorts and routes to the right pipeline.
Extract evidence. Workers pull metadata, captions, transcripts, OCR text, speech, and browser-rendered content.
Score the signals. The engine evaluates misinformation, scam, AI content, manipulation, confidence, and evidence quality.
Show the result. The user receives a compact, score-first card with plain-language explanations.

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 4. System architecture
chunks.text:
4. System architecture
The first version ran everything inside a single web process. That broke quickly: video download, Whisper transcription, and
headless browsers are memory-hungry, and the small Fly machine was killed by out-of-memory errors under load. The fix was an
architectural split between a control plane and a data plane .
Control plane · Fly.io
FastAPI Link intake, /api/analyze , job APIs
SQLite queue Persistent volume at /data/jobs.db , duplicate-job reuse
Scoring engine Deterministic six-signal aggregation
Dashboard Queue health, worker lanes, job detail
↓ workers claim jobs · ↑ workers upload evidence artifacts
Data plane · Oracle Cloud VMs
Lane A Instagram + TikTok · Playwright, Tesseract OCR, faster-whisper, yt-dlp
Lane B Instagram + TikTok · parallel capacity with warm Chromium reuse
Lane C YouTube only · ffmpeg, browser fallback, OCR, ASR
↓ final JSON report
Output
Result card Score, risk flags, claim notes, evidence coverage
The request lifecycle follows five API steps: the client submits a URL ( POST /api/jobs ), a worker claims it
( POST /api/jobs/claim ), the worker performs rich ingestion and uploads artifacts
( POST /api/jobs/{id}/artifacts ), the server computes the final score, and the client polls for the result
( GET /api/jobs/{id} ). This keeps the public web tier small and cheap while pushing expensive work to machines
that can afford it.

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 4. System architecture
chunks.text:
A second design decision was lane isolation . YouTube jobs are frequently slowed by anti-bot checks. When
all platforms shared one worker, a single stuck YouTube job blocked Instagram and TikTok behind it. Moving YouTube to a
dedicated lane (Lane C) and running two parallel lanes for the other platforms removed that head-of-line blocking.
Go deeper: engineering notes
For the code-level version of this section, including atomic job claiming with BEGIN IMMEDIATE , platform
routing filters, adapter interfaces, and stale-job recovery, read
Building a Multi-Lane Data Plane for Short-Form Video Credibility Analysis [13]
in my @Field Notes .
Figure 2. Control plane on Fly.io, data plane on Oracle VMs, with three isolated worker lanes.

chunks.heading: 5. Evidence extraction
chunks.text:
5. Evidence extraction
Each platform exposes different data and blocks automated access in different ways, so each needed its own pipeline that
still returns the same evidence contract: caption , transcript , ocr ,
asr , and notes .
Platform Primary path Fallbacks Status
Instagram
Worker-side @Playwright browser render with authenticated session
Screenshot OCR, media download + local Whisper ASR
Strongest
TikTok
Public metadata + browser-rendered page recovery
Screenshot OCR, media URL discovery + ASR, fast-mode early exit
Stable
YouTube Shorts

An important engineering lesson was that public HTML is often useless. Instagram typically returns a generic app shell to

evidence only appeared once a headless browser rendered the page the way a human would see it, and richer audio only appeared
once the worker had an authenticated session for media download.
The system also counts what it found. Every result includes an evidence_coverage object with total tokens,

high . That object is what lets the scoring engine, and the user, reason about how much to trust the output.

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 6. Claim verification
chunks.text:
6. Claim verification
Once text is extracted, the system identifies candidate claims and checks them against a trusted-source retrieval corpus.
The baseline verifier is fully open-source: it retrieves relevant evidence chunks, applies lexical support and refute checks
with citations, and returns not_enough_evidence when support is weak.
Hosted and local LLMs are layered on top only when the evidence justifies it . I tested three options:
@OpenAI ( gpt-5-mini )
for hosted reasoning, @OpenRouter
free-tier models, and @Ollama
running Qwen models locally on the worker. The local route proved impractical on a 1 GB Always Free VM, so production
uses OpenAI behind a platform-aware gate:
Platform Min. evidence tokens Min. evidence level
Instagram 60 medium
TikTok 50 medium
YouTube Shorts 20 low
Table 2. LLM gating thresholds. Below the gate, the system falls back to open-source heuristics.
Key design decision
The LLM produces structured claim assessments as JSON. It never writes the credibility score. Keeping the final number in deterministic application code means the score is reproducible, auditable, and not subject to prompt drift.

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 7. Scoring model
chunks.text:
7. Scoring model
The scoring engine converts extracted evidence and claim assessments into six component signals, each on a 0 to 100 scale
where higher means more risk: misinformation , scam , manipulation ,
uncertainty , evidence-quality penalty , and a separate generation-origin
(AI vs human) flag. An analysis confidence value then decides how much the final score is allowed to move
away from neutral.
# 1. Weighted risk penalty (weights sum to 1.0)
penalty = 0.34·misinformation + 0.24·scam + 0.18·manipulation
+ 0.12·uncertainty + 0.12·evidence_quality_penalty
raw = 100 − penalty
# 2. Analysis confidence c ∈ [0, 1]
c = 0.28·token_signal + 0.22·transcript_signal + 0.20·decisive_claims
+ 0.15·citation_signal + 0.15·max(modality_signal, coverage_signal)
# 3. Shrink toward a neutral anchor when evidence is thin
credibility = raw · c + 52 · (1 − c)
The third step is the heart of RQ3. With rich evidence, c approaches 1 and the score reflects the detected
risks. With almost no evidence, c approaches 0 and the score converges on 52 , a deliberately
neutral value that communicates "insufficient information" rather than "safe" or "dangerous". This is a simple form of
Bayesian-style shrinkage: the prior is neutrality, and only evidence earns the right to move away from it.

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 7.1 Component rules
chunks.text:
7.1 Component rules
Misinformation averages per-claim penalties: refuted claims add 60 plus up to 35 points by confidence; unverifiable claims add a smaller penalty; supported claims add almost nothing.
Scam scales with detected fraud cues such as guaranteed returns, urgency, and "DM me" patterns (20 points per cue above a base).
Manipulation weights strong synthetic cues (deepfake, face swap, voice clone) above generic AI mentions, plus an optional external detector score.
Evidence-quality penalty blends token depth (40%), transcript presence (20%), decisive claims (23%), and citation coverage (17%).

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 7.2 Generation-origin calibration
chunks.text:
7.2 Generation-origin calibration
To estimate whether a clip is AI-generated, I built labeled data from two
@Kaggle sources: an AI Shorts
dataset by @aibuttonfoundation
and a human Shorts dataset by @prince7489 .
When the human dataset turned out to contain synthetic IDs, I replaced it with labels scraped from real public human
channels. A logistic calibrator trained on 183 rows is blended (70/30) with the heuristic score.
Explicit self-disclosure overrides calibration. If the caption says "#aigenerated" or "made with AI", the generation-origin
score is floored at 85; weaker tags floor it at 65. When such a clip also has low evidence, credibility is capped at 44 or 49
respectively. This fixed an early bug where clearly labeled AI videos were being calibrated back to "human-generated likely".
Figure 3. From input to output: live evidence, reference datasets, analysis models, and the final scored card.

9. Evaluation & results
All numbers below come from reproducible report files in the repository's reports/ directory. I report failures
alongside successes, because the failures are what shaped the architecture.

chunks.text:
9.1 Phase 1 readiness gates
Before expanding beyond YouTube, I defined four pass/fail gates and ran a balanced, seeded benchmark of 100 videos
(seed 20260303 ).
Gate Result Threshold Outcome
Ingestion success rate 46% ≥ 85% Fail
"Not enough evidence" rate 97.8% ≤ 40% Fail
Score standard deviation 4.10 ≥ 8.0 Fail
Queue reliability 97% ≥ 95% Pass
Table 3. Phase 1 readiness benchmark, March 4, 2026 (n = 100, balanced AI/human).
The pattern was diagnostic. The queue worked, but the system could not see enough of each video to say anything decisive,
so scores clustered tightly around neutral. That result redirected effort away from scoring tweaks and toward ingestion:
browser rendering, authenticated workers, OCR, and ASR.

On a 780-link YouTube batch, every job completed. Because YouTube's anti-bot friction left most videos with only about 19
tokens of evidence, 754 of 780 scores landed below 55. This is the intended behavior: the system declined to make strong
claims it could not support, which directly answers RQ3.

On a small three-video comparison, enabling gated OpenAI claim assessment raised average credibility by +6.33 points and

chunks.heading: 10.1 Evidence is the product
chunks.text:
10.1 Evidence is the product
The single biggest lever on output quality was not the model; it was how much of the video the system could actually see.
Every major jump in usefulness (Instagram's 131x evidence increase, the move from flat to differentiated scores) came from
better extraction. For anyone building trust tooling, ingestion deserves at least as much investment as inference.

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 10.2 Honest uncertainty beats confident guessing
chunks.text:
10.2 Honest uncertainty beats confident guessing
A credibility tool that confidently mislabels a video does more harm than one that says "I can't tell". Anchoring low-evidence
results to a neutral 52 and surfacing evidence coverage next to every score made the system's limits visible to the user
instead of hiding them.

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 10.3 LLMs as components, not oracles
chunks.text:
10.3 LLMs as components, not oracles
Constraining the LLM to structured claim assessment, gating it on evidence thresholds, and keeping the final score in code gave
the benefits of language reasoning without sacrificing reproducibility. It also controlled cost: the model is only called when
there is enough material for it to add value.

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 10.4 Product lessons
chunks.text:
10.4 Product lessons
Benchmarks as decision gates. Pre-committing to pass/fail thresholds turned a disappointing result into a clear roadmap.
Architecture follows constraints. Free-tier memory limits forced the control/data plane split, which turned out to be the right design anyway.
Isolate the slowest dependency. Giving YouTube its own lane protected the experience on the other two platforms.
Operational visibility matters. The live dashboard made it possible to demo, debug, and explain the system to non-engineers.

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 11. Limitations, threats to validity & ethics
chunks.text:
11. Limitations, threats to validity & ethics
Platform access. YouTube remains the weakest path due to anti-bot and sign-in friction. Richer Instagram and TikTok extraction depends on authenticated worker sessions, which raises terms-of-service and sustainability questions for any production deployment.
Hand-set weights. The six-signal weights were chosen by design reasoning and iteration, not learned from a large labeled credibility dataset.
Small labeled samples. Several evaluations (LLM comparison, generation-origin check) use small samples and should be read as directional.
Corpus coverage. Claim verification can only be as good as the trusted-source corpus it retrieves from.
Language and modality. OCR and ASR work best on clear, English-language content. Visual deepfake detection is not yet performed directly on frames.
Curated demo layer. A small override list keeps a handful of presentation examples consistent during live demos. Benchmark figures in Section 9 come from batch runs, not from that list.
Responsible use
CrediClip is a decision-support signal, not a verdict. A low score means "look closer", not "this is false". It is designed to help people and moderators prioritize attention, with the evidence visible so a human can make the final call.

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 12. Applications
chunks.text:
12. Applications
Moderation triage: surface suspect videos with evidence-backed reasoning so human reviewers start with the highest-risk queue.
Trust-and-safety API: a credibility layer that platforms or brand-safety tools can call inside existing workflows.
Fact-checking support: faster screening of high-volume video so fact-checkers spend time where it matters.
Media literacy: transparent credibility framing that teaches end users what signals to look for.

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 13. Future work
chunks.text:
13. Future work
Formal evaluation of the manipulation signal on FaceForensics++, DFDC, and ASVspoof [3] [4] [5] .
Vector retrieval (FAISS or pgvector) and a larger trusted corpus to raise claim-verification recall.
Learned signal weights from a labeled credibility dataset, with calibration curves reported per platform.
Postgres-backed analysis history, authentication, and role-based dashboards for moderators and researchers.
Larger worker VMs to make local LLM inference viable and reduce dependence on hosted APIs.
Multilingual OCR and ASR support.

chunks.pageTitle: CrediClip: Evidence-Aware Credibility Scoring for Short-Form Video · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: 14. Conclusion
chunks.text:
14. Conclusion
CrediClip shows that a small team, or in this case a single product-minded builder, can ship a working, multi-platform
credibility system on free and low-cost infrastructure. On the three research questions: link-only evidence recovery is
feasible but platform-dependent (RQ1); a deterministic, six-signal score with visible evidence makes credibility explainable
and reproducible (RQ2); and shrinking toward a neutral anchor under thin evidence is a simple, effective guard against false
confidence (RQ3).
The broader takeaway is a product one. In trust tooling, the most valuable thing a system can do is be honest about what it
knows. Link in, evidence out, clearer trust signal.

MrBeast: Predicting YouTube Engagement from Metadata
Can a creator predict engagement before uploading, using only things they control, such as title, length, and
timing? This BAN 612 project tested that question on MrBeast's channel with interpretable machine learning.
Date
Fall 2025
Course
BAN 612 · Cal State East Bay
Data
250 uploads via YouTube Data API v3
Deck
11 slides
Python
YouTube Data API
Random Forest
Gradient Boosting
SHAP
250 MrBeast videos analyzed
4 models compared with 5-fold cross-validation

Method
Pipeline: API, cleaning, feature engineering, EDA, modeling, then SHAP interpretation.
Features: duration in seconds, publish hour and weekday, a peak-hour flag (18–22h), a Shorts flag, and title length.
EDA: views are heavy-tailed (so log-transformed), duration has a non-linear effect, and title length shows a small positive correlation.
Models: linear and logistic regression baselines against random forest and gradient boosting, scored with R² and ROC-AUC.
Findings
Performance: tree models modestly outperformed the linear baselines, and their bigger value was interpretability.
Top SHAP drivers: duration, the Shorts flag, publish hour, the peak-hour flag, and title length.
Local example: a 45-second Short posted at 19:00 with a balanced title was predicted high-engagement.

chunks.text:
Building a Multi-Lane Data Plane for Short-Form Video Credibility Analysis
How I separated CrediClip's web control plane from platform-specific evidence workers to analyze YouTube Shorts, Instagram Reels, and TikTok videos reliably.
Author
Ali Raza
Published
October 14, 2026
Reading time
10 min read
Python
FastAPI
System Architecture
AI
On this page
Short-form video looks simple from the outside: paste a link, wait briefly, and receive a credibility score. The engineering behind that interaction is less simple. YouTube Shorts, Instagram Reels, and TikTok expose different metadata, apply different anti-bot controls, and fail in different ways. A single request handler that tries to download media, transcribe audio, scan frames, retrieve evidence, and score a claim quickly becomes slow and fragile.
I encountered this problem while building CrediClip , my capstone project for credibility analysis of short-form video. The most important architectural decision was to separate the system into two parts:
a control plane that accepts links, stores job state, exposes status APIs, and returns results;
a data plane made of background workers that perform platform-specific evidence extraction and analysis.

chunks.pageTitle: Building a Multi-Lane Data Plane for Short-Form Video Credibility Analysis · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: Building a Multi-Lane Data Plane for Short-Form Video Credibility Analysis
chunks.text:
Within the data plane, I introduced worker lanes . Each lane can accept or reject jobs by platform, allowing expensive or unreliable workloads to be isolated without duplicating the entire application.
This article explains why the architecture was necessary, how it works, and what I learned from implementing it.
The code excerpts below are shortened from the working project for readability. The complete implementation is available in the CrediClip repository .

chunks.pageTitle: Building a Multi-Lane Data Plane for Short-Form Video Credibility Analysis · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: The problem with a single synchronous pipeline
chunks.text:
The problem with a single synchronous pipeline
The first version of the application followed a straightforward flow:
browser request
-> fetch platform page
-> extract caption and transcript
-> run OCR or speech transcription
-> analyze credibility
-> return response
That design works for a controlled demo, but it creates several production problems.
First, evidence extraction is much slower than ordinary web processing. A video may require browser rendering, media download, frame sampling, OCR, or automatic speech recognition. Holding an HTTP request open during all of those stages makes timeouts much more likely.
Second, the platforms do not behave alike. Instagram may expose useful rendered metadata while withholding the media file. TikTok may require a browser session or cookies. YouTube may return captions successfully for one video and produce an anti-bot challenge for the next. Treating those workloads as identical means one platform’s failure mode can consume all available capacity.
Third, the workload is resource-heavy. Browser processes, media decoding, OCR, and transcription compete for memory and CPU. Running them inside the public web process risks slowing every visitor or terminating the process entirely.
The solution was not simply “add more servers.” The system needed a clear boundary between coordinating work and performing work.

chunks.pageTitle: Building a Multi-Lane Data Plane for Short-Form Video Credibility Analysis · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: Control plane versus data plane
chunks.text:
Control plane versus data plane
The control plane is intentionally lightweight. It performs four main tasks:
normalize and validate submitted URLs;
create or reuse jobs in a persistent queue;
allow workers to claim and update jobs;
let the client poll one job until it completes or fails.
The data plane performs the expensive operations:
identify the source platform;
retrieve captions, transcripts, metadata, and media where available;
run browser-assisted extraction, OCR, frame scanning, or speech transcription;
calculate evidence coverage and credibility signals;
send artifacts or a completed result back to the control plane.
The resulting flow is:
User
|
v
FastAPI control plane
|
+--> SQLite job queue
|
+--> Instagram/TikTok lane A
+--> Instagram/TikTok lane B
+--> YouTube Shorts lane
|
v
captions + ASR + OCR + metadata
|
v
credibility result
|
v
SQLite job record
This separation provides two useful guarantees. The public API remains responsive even when extraction is slow, and a failing platform can be isolated to its own worker lane.

chunks.pageTitle: Building a Multi-Lane Data Plane for Short-Form Video Credibility Analysis · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: Step 1: represent analysis as a durable job
chunks.text:
Step 1: represent analysis as a durable job
When the frontend submits a video URL, the API does not immediately perform rich extraction. It creates or reuses a queue job:
@ app . post ( "/api/jobs" , response_model = JobResponse )
def create_analysis_job ( request : JobCreateRequest ) -> JobResponse :
normalized_url , _ = normalize_input_url ( str ( request . url ))
job = create_or_reuse_job ( normalized_url )
return JobResponse ( ** job )
The job record stores a small state machine:
queued -> processing -> completed
\-> failed
For the MVP, I used SQLite rather than introducing a separate queue product. That was a deliberate tradeoff. The project needed durable state, atomic claiming, simple backup, and low operating cost more than it needed distributed throughput.
The table stores the URL, status, worker identity, extracted caption and transcript, diagnostic notes, result JSON, error information, and timestamps. This makes the queue useful not only for scheduling but also for observability.
The API also reuses an active or recently completed job for the same URL. That prevents repeated clicks from creating duplicate browser and transcription work. A result-version marker ensures that stale results are not reused after scoring logic changes.

chunks.pageTitle: Building a Multi-Lane Data Plane for Short-Form Video Credibility Analysis · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: Step 2: claim jobs atomically
chunks.text:
Step 2: claim jobs atomically
Multiple workers poll the same API. If two workers read the same queued record at the same time, they could both analyze it. To prevent that, the claim operation starts an immediate SQLite transaction, selects an eligible job, and changes its status before releasing the lock.
def claim_next_job ( worker_id , include_platforms = None , exclude_platforms = None ):
recover_stale_jobs ()
include = set ( include_platforms or [])
exclude = set ( exclude_platforms or [])
with _connect () as conn :
conn . execute ( "BEGIN IMMEDIATE" )
rows = conn . execute (
"""
SELECT * FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'queued'
ORDER BY created_at ASC
LIMIT 200
"""
). fetchall ()
selected = None
for candidate in rows :
platform = _job_platform ( candidate [ "url" ])
if include and platform not in include :
continue
if exclude and platform in exclude :
continue
selected = candidate
break
if selected is None :
return None
conn . execute (
"""
UPDATE jobs
SET status = 'processing', worker_id = ?, updated_at = ?
WHERE id = ?
""" ,
( worker_id , _now_iso (), selected [ "id" ]),
)
conn . commit ()
return get_job ( selected [ "id" ])
BEGIN IMMEDIATE is important here. It serializes competing writers during the short claim operation. This is enough for the scale of the MVP and avoids adding Redis or a message broker solely for locking.

chunks.pageTitle: Building a Multi-Lane Data Plane for Short-Form Video Credibility Analysis · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: Step 3: create lanes with routing filters
chunks.text:
Step 3: create lanes with routing filters
A lane is not a separate codebase. It is the same worker started with a different routing policy.
parser . add_argument ( "--include-platforms" , default = "" )
parser . add_argument ( "--exclude-platforms" , default = "" )
payload = { "worker_id" : worker_id }
if include_platforms :
payload [ "include_platforms" ] = include_platforms
if exclude_platforms :
payload [ "exclude_platforms" ] = exclude_platforms
response = client . post ( f " { api_base } /api/jobs/claim" , json = payload )
job = response . json (). get ( "job" )
The deployed topology used two general lanes for Instagram and TikTok and one dedicated YouTube Shorts lane:
# General evidence lane
python scripts/queue_worker.py \
--worker-id oracle-worker-1 \
--exclude-platforms youtube_shorts \
--ingest-mode rich
# Dedicated YouTube lane
python scripts/queue_worker.py \
--worker-id oracle-worker-youtube \
--include-platforms youtube_shorts \
--ingest-mode rich
YouTube was separated because its anti-bot and authentication behavior differed from Instagram and TikTok. If YouTube extraction stalled, it could no longer occupy every worker. The general lanes remained available for the other platforms.

chunks.heading: Step 3: create lanes with routing filters
chunks.text: The same mechanism can support future policies without rewriting the queue: a high-priority lane, a GPU-backed transcription lane, or a lane restricted to jobs that already contain transcripts.

chunks.pageTitle: Building a Multi-Lane Data Plane for Short-Form Video Credibility Analysis · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: Step 4: use one interface with platform-specific adapters
chunks.text: The evidence object also records coverage signals such as caption tokens, transcript tokens, OCR tokens, ASR tokens, and an overall evidence level. That information affects uncertainty and prevents a sparse extraction from being presented with the same confidence as a high-coverage analysis.

chunks.pageTitle: Building a Multi-Lane Data Plane for Short-Form Video Credibility Analysis · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: Step 5: decide where analysis runs
chunks.text:
Step 5: decide where analysis runs
The worker supports two modes:
local analysis : extract evidence and run the complete scoring pipeline on the worker;
server analysis : extract evidence on the worker, then send artifacts to the API for scoring.
if analysis_mode == "local" :
result = await analyze_video (
AnalyzeRequest (
url = url ,
caption = caption ,
transcript = transcript ,
ingest_evidence = ingest_evidence ,
)
)
post_complete_result ( job_id , caption , transcript , result )
else :
post_artifacts ( job_id , caption , transcript , ingest_evidence )
This switch made deployment more flexible. A small web host could remain lightweight while a VM performed rich ingestion and scoring. Alternatively, the worker could upload artifacts to a stronger analysis server. The queue contract stayed the same in both cases.

chunks.pageTitle: Building a Multi-Lane Data Plane for Short-Form Video Credibility Analysis · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: Step 6: design for failure, not only success
chunks.text:
Step 6: design for failure, not only success
Background processing creates a specific reliability problem: a worker can claim a job and then disappear. Without recovery, that job remains in processing forever.
CrediClip periodically checks processing jobs and requeues any that have exceeded a configurable stale threshold:
def recover_stale_jobs ():
now = datetime . now ( timezone . utc )
recovered = []
with _connect () as conn :
rows = conn . execute (
"SELECT id, updated_at FROM jobs WHERE status = 'processing'"
). fetchall ()
for row in rows :
age = now - datetime . fromisoformat ( row [ "updated_at" ])
if age . total_seconds () >= PROCESSING_STALE_SEC :
recovered . append ( row [ "id" ])
for job_id in recovered :
conn . execute (
"""
UPDATE jobs
SET status = 'queued', worker_id = NULL, updated_at = ?
WHERE id = ?
""" ,
( _now_iso (), job_id ),
)
conn . commit ()
Timeouts are handled at the ingestion and analysis boundaries, and failures are written back to the job record. The frontend can therefore distinguish “still working” from “failed,” and operators can inspect the reason instead of searching through only terminal logs.

chunks.pageTitle: Building a Multi-Lane Data Plane for Short-Form Video Credibility Analysis · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: What the lane model improved
chunks.text:
What the lane model improved
The lane architecture improved the project in four practical ways.
Isolation. YouTube-specific failures no longer consumed all worker capacity.
Responsiveness. The web layer handled short API operations while media processing happened elsewhere.
Observability. Every job recorded its state, assigned worker, evidence volume, notes, result, and error.
Cost control. The MVP could use SQLite and small worker VMs instead of a managed queue, distributed database, or large always-on server.
It also made the system easier to explain. The score was no longer the output of a single opaque model call. It was the final stage of an observable pipeline that collected evidence, measured coverage, assessed signals, and recorded uncertainty.

chunks.pageTitle: Building a Multi-Lane Data Plane for Short-Form Video Credibility Analysis · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: Scoring, confidence, and evaluation
chunks.text:
Scoring, confidence, and evaluation
The final score is computed in deterministic application code. LLMs can provide structured claim assessments when evidence thresholds are met. Low analysis confidence shrinks scores toward a neutral anchor of 52, while evidence coverage describes the recovered inputs. That behavior is a design choice, not an independently validated probability.
In the March 11, 2026 YouTube batch, all 780 jobs eventually completed, including two retried links, but 759 results (97.3%) were low evidence. In a separate 19-link Instagram comparison between March 11 and March 13, mean evidence tokens rose from 1.0 to 130.9. These measurements describe completion and evidence recovery. They do not establish credibility accuracy.
The evaluation article links the underlying reports and distinguishes these measurements from independently labeled assessment quality. Stronger labeled evaluation and confidence calibration remain necessary.

chunks.pageTitle: Building a Multi-Lane Data Plane for Short-Form Video Credibility Analysis · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: Tradeoffs and limits
chunks.text:
Tradeoffs and limits
The design is intentionally pragmatic, but it has limits.
SQLite is suitable for a small deployment with a limited number of concurrent writers. At higher scale, the job store should move to PostgreSQL and a dedicated queue such as Redis, RabbitMQ, or a managed equivalent.
Polling is simple but introduces repeated requests and small delays. Server-Sent Events or WebSockets could improve result delivery for a larger interactive product.
Platform adapters remain dependent on external websites whose markup, authentication, and anti-automation controls can change. The lane model contains those failures, but it cannot eliminate them.
Finally, routing by platform is only a first-level policy. A mature system could route by evidence requirements, expected duration, account/session availability, or resource class.

chunks.pageTitle: Building a Multi-Lane Data Plane for Short-Form Video Credibility Analysis · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: Lessons from building the data plane
chunks.text:
Lessons from building the data plane
The main lesson was that credibility analysis is not only a modeling problem. Before scoring can be trusted, the system must reliably collect and describe the evidence that reached the model.
Separating the control plane from the data plane created a stable boundary between user-facing coordination and unpredictable media work. Adding lanes then turned platform differences into explicit routing decisions rather than hidden exceptions inside one large process.
For an MVP, the best architecture is not necessarily the one with the most infrastructure. It is the smallest architecture that makes failure visible, protects the user-facing path, and leaves clear upgrade points. In CrediClip, a FastAPI control plane, a durable SQLite queue, and lane-aware Python workers were enough to achieve that goal.

chunks.text:
What 780 completed video jobs taught me about AI product quality
How evidence coverage, readiness benchmarks, and explicit uncertainty shaped the CrediClip roadmap.
Author
Ali Raza
Published
October 26, 2026
Reading time
6 min read
AI Product Management
Evaluation
Evidence Extraction
FastAPI
On this page
A completed job is an easy result to count. In an AI application, understanding what that completed job contains takes more work.
I encountered that distinction while building CrediClip, a system that accepts a public short-form video link and returns a credibility score, risk flags, claim assessments, and an evidence-coverage breakdown. The product brought together several different problems: getting access to a video, recovering its text and speech, assessing claims, and presenting a result a person could interpret.
In the March 11, 2026 YouTube batch, all 780 jobs eventually completed, including two retried links. Yet 759 of 780 results, or 97.3%, were flagged as low evidence. The pipeline finished its work while recovering little information from most inputs. That result became a useful way to explain what the evaluation established and where the product still needed improvement.

chunks.page: Field note: CrediClip AI product quality
chunks.pageTitle: What 780 completed video jobs taught me about AI product quality · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: The benchmark that redirected the roadmap
chunks.text:
The benchmark that redirected the roadmap
Before expanding the product, I ran a balanced, seeded benchmark of 100 videos against four readiness gates on March 4, 2026. Ingestion success was 46%, against a threshold of at least 85%. Among the 46 inputs with successful ingestion, 45 had insufficient evidence for claim verification: 97.8%, against a target of no more than 40%. Score variation also fell below the chosen threshold. The supplied queue reliability measurement passed at 97%.
These were readiness thresholds I had chosen for the project, rather than universal standards for credibility products. Their value was in making a decision concrete. A functioning queue did not resolve the lack of evidence. Changing score weights would still leave the system working with sparse inputs.
The results redirected my effort toward ingestion: browser rendering, on-screen text extraction, speech recognition, and platform-specific recovery paths. Evaluation gave me a reason to change the roadmap and a way to explain that choice.

chunks.page: Field note: CrediClip AI product quality
chunks.pageTitle: What 780 completed video jobs taught me about AI product quality · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: Evidence recovery became a product concern
chunks.text:
Evidence recovery became a product concern
Short-form video exposes important information through several channels. A caption may contain context, speech may contain the main claim, and text on a frame may carry information missing from both. Losing a channel can change what the system is able to assess.
The extraction paths also differed by platform. Public metadata could be thin, browser rendering could recover additional text, and media access could determine whether speech recognition was possible. I brought those outputs into a shared evidence structure so the product could show what had been recovered.
In the 19-link Instagram benchmark comparing March 11 and March 13, 2026, average evidence tokens increased from 1.0 to 130.9 after the ingestion redesign. That was an improvement in recovered evidence on a small benchmark. It did not measure whether credibility judgments had become more accurate. Keeping that distinction attached to the number matters when describing the result.

chunks.page: Field note: CrediClip AI product quality
chunks.pageTitle: What 780 completed video jobs taught me about AI product quality · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: The architecture had to support the extraction work
chunks.text:
The architecture had to support the extraction work
The first version performed heavy processing inside the web process. Video downloads, headless browsers, and speech recognition created memory pressure on the small hosting instance.
I separated the lightweight FastAPI control plane from the workers doing heavy extraction. The web tier handled requests, queue state, scoring, and results. Workers handled platform-specific ingestion and returned artifacts for assessment.
I also separated YouTube work into its own lane after slow or blocked jobs interfered with the other platforms. This was a decision about the user’s wait as well as infrastructure. An unpredictable dependency on one platform should not hold up unrelated work.

chunks.page: Field note: CrediClip AI product quality
chunks.pageTitle: What 780 completed video jobs taught me about AI product quality · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: Showing uncertainty in the output
chunks.text:
Showing uncertainty in the output
CrediClip needed a way to represent an assessment made from limited evidence. I kept the final score in deterministic application code and used an analysis-confidence value to control how far the result moved from a neutral anchor of 52.
When evidence is thin, that rule keeps the score near the anchor. The interface also presents evidence coverage so a reader can see the basis for the assessment. This is a designed behavior; its usefulness and calibration still need stronger evaluation. A precise-looking score does not by itself establish a precise judgment.
LLMs have a narrower role in the workflow. They can produce structured claim assessments when evidence thresholds are met. They do not directly write the final credibility number. That boundary makes the scoring rule easier to inspect and keeps the role of the model explicit.

chunks.page: Field note: CrediClip AI product quality
chunks.pageTitle: What 780 completed video jobs taught me about AI product quality · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: Three questions for evaluating the product
chunks.text:
Three questions for evaluating the product
The work left me with three separate questions. Did the processing complete? Did it recover enough relevant evidence? Did the assessment match an independently established judgment?
The 780-link batch answered the first question for that run and exposed limitations in the second. It did not settle the third. Answering that would require stronger labeled evaluation, careful separation of calibration and test data, and reporting across platforms and content types.
Several limitations remain in CrediClip: uneven platform access, hand-set scoring weights, restricted retrieval coverage, and small labeled evaluations. The case study also discloses curated presentation examples. Those examples are separate from the reported batch results.
For me, the product lesson was to connect each metric to a decision. Completion helped evaluate the processing workflow. Evidence coverage helped identify the next ingestion work. Stronger independent evaluation is needed to assess the credibility judgments themselves.
Building the workflow and documenting those distinctions gave me a clearer view of what I had shipped, what its outputs meant, and what I needed to learn next.

Author

On this page
A caller asks a simple question: “How much to clean the windows on my house?” Answering it well is harder than it sounds. The office has a phone number, an address, and maybe a rough description of the home. The price needs to be fair, consistent across agents, and ready before the caller loses interest.
I built the Blue Ocean Estimate Tool during my summer 2026 Business Operations Internship at Blue Ocean Window Cleaning, a residential and commercial cleaning company in San Diego. It is an internal Next.js app that produces phone-ready quotes for new customers from phone and Angi leads. This article explains the part that does most of the work but never appears on screen: the data plane that turns raw job history into the files the quote engine reads.
The code excerpts below are shortened from the working project for readability. Figures are aggregates from the project’s own validation reports. No customer-level data appears in this article.

chunks.pageTitle: Building the Data Plane Behind a Phone-Ready Window-Cleaning Quote · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: The quoting problem
chunks.text:
The quoting problem
Before the tool, quoting relied on individual judgment and spreadsheets. Two agents could quote the same house differently, and neither could easily explain why. The business already had the raw material for something better: years of completed jobs in Housecall Pro (HCP), its field-service platform. That history was messy, though.
Mixed tickets. A single job might combine window cleaning with solar panels, gutters, screens, or pressure washing. Its total says little about the price of windows alone.
Missing property data. Jobs record an address, not the square footage, bedrooms, or stories that drive effort.
Unstructured hours. Time on site often lives in free-text descriptions rather than clean fields.
Scope ambiguity. “Inside only,” “outside only,” “select windows,” and “partial” all mean very different amounts of work.
The goal was a quote an agent could give in under a minute, with a range, a confidence signal, and a plain-language explanation of how the number was reached.

chunks.pageTitle: Building the Data Plane Behind a Phone-Ready Window-Cleaning Quote · Field notes · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: Two-plane architecture
chunks.text:
Two-plane architecture
I split the system into two planes with very different jobs.
The data plane is a set of offline Node.js scripts. It pulls job history, cleans and enriches it, fits models, validates them, and promotes the results into versioned JSON files.
The quote path is the Next.js app. It never touches raw history. On each request it reads the promoted JSON, looks up the property, and computes a price.
Housecall Pro API ──> sync ──> clean ──> enrich ──> calibrate ──> train
|
office corrections ──┐ v
├──> validate ──> promote
| |
| v
| data/*.json artifacts
| |
Caller address ──> parcel lookup ──> quote engine <─────────────────┘
|
v
price + range + confidence + explanation
|
└──> office log ──> corrections
This boundary keeps expensive preparation outside the request path. API pagination, text parsing, and regression fitting happen offline, so a failed preparation run can be inspected before its artifacts replace the files used for quotes. Artifact promotion and concurrent writes still need explicit controls.

Step 1: sync completed jobs from Housecall Pro
The pipeline starts with the HCP Public API. The sync script pulls completed jobs for a time window, caches the raw responses, and merges them into the same CSV shape as a manual HCP export. Keeping one export format meant every later stage worked whether the data came from the API or a spreadsheet download.
node ml/sync-hcp-api.mjs --days = 180 --with-line-items # incremental pull
node ml/sync-hcp-api.mjs --comps-only # rebuild comps offline
node ml/sync-hcp-api.mjs --max-pages = 5 --dry-run # safe test run
The --comps-only flag rebuilds downstream files from the cached export without calling the API again. That made iteration cheap: I could change cleaning rules and regenerate everything in seconds. The most recent sync covered 11,482 jobs , with on-site hours recovered for 7,595 of them and technician counts for 8,971 .

chunks.text:
Step 4: recover hours and rates from descriptions
Price alone does not explain effort. A parser extracts price-relevant signals from job descriptions and API job objects: on-site hours, technician count, and per-pane notes. Durations outside a plausible range (under 15 minutes or over 16 hours) are discarded rather than trusted.
From these signals the pipeline computes dollars per hour by scope . That rate becomes an independent pricing signal for brand-new addresses: predicted hours multiplied by the historical hourly rate.

chunks.heading: Step 5: train the exterior model and derive the rest
chunks.text: The exterior model is an ordinary least squares regression on square footage, bedrooms, bathrooms, property type, and lead source. Its training set blends two sources. A capped base sample of cleaned historical jobs carries modest weights, with parcel-matched rows weighted higher than unmatched ones. A small gold set of 18 jobs from a manually maintained job-tracking sheet, with clean paid amounts and durations, carries a much heavier weight so it can steer the fit. On that gold set the model reached a mean absolute error of about $58 , with two-thirds of quotes within 25% of the actual price.

chunks.text: Two design choices made the output usable on a call. First, every quote returns a step-by-step explanation (“Step 1: exterior regression $X; Step 4: HCP lookup, n jobs, 40% blend…”), shown in a derivation panel, so an agent can defend the number. Second, a confidence score rises when the parcel matched, when the caller confirmed square footage, or when many historical jobs back the lookup cell. Low confidence prompts the agent to confirm details instead of guessing.

The two columns use different job sets, so this is not a controlled experiment. The early column is the first validation pass. The live-predictor column, three days later, scored the enriched training set with the full blended engine, including lookups and address comps. The later run combines cleaning, enrichment, and comparable-job signals, but these evaluations do not isolate the contribution of each change.
The numbers also need an honest caveat. The live predictor uses address comps built from the same history it is scored on, so repeat addresses look better than a truly new customer would. The reported mean bias was about $23 under the reference price. This is an observed error, not evidence that underpricing is desirable. A separate check on 17 known townhome units from an HOA project landed within 10% for 82% of units; the small, specific sample does not establish generalization.

chunks.heading: Tradeoffs and limits
chunks.text:
Tradeoffs and limits
The architecture is deliberately small, and that has costs.
Files instead of a database. JSON artifacts are easy to inspect and version, but they assume a single writer and a modest data size. A larger operation would move job history to PostgreSQL and schedule the pipeline.
Address matching is heuristic. Normalized street strings and fuzzy parcel queries require match-quality checks. Parcel coverage was 29% in the reported run; the evaluation does not isolate its effect on accuracy.
Evaluation is optimistic for repeat addresses. The next step is a time-based holdout that scores only addresses first seen after the training cutoff.
The gold set is small. Eighteen heavily weighted jobs can strongly affect the fit. More representative labels and held-out evaluation are needed to assess stability.
Customer data needs a separate home. Training inputs contain customer-level records. In a next iteration I would keep raw exports in private storage and commit only aggregated, anonymized artifacts.

chunks.heading: Lessons learned
chunks.text:
Lessons learned
The biggest lesson was to make data assumptions inspectable: which jobs count as window cleaning, which size field describes the house, and how hours are recovered from free text. The retrospective comparisons do not isolate the effect of those choices from model changes or repeat-address evidence.
The second lesson was to treat explainability as a product feature, not a nice-to-have. An agent will not trust a number they cannot explain to a customer. Showing each pricing step, with its source and weight, gives staff a basis for reviewing and correcting a quote.
The resulting design uses scripts to write versioned JSON artifacts for a small Next.js app. That makes the calculation inspectable and identifies future storage and promotion work. It does not, by itself, establish business savings, adoption, or a reduction in quoting time.

chunks.pageTitle: Raasta: an instrumented product experiment · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: The decision and my role
chunks.text:
The decision and my role
Should an intake form show every field at once or guide the participant through a short sequence? I treated cognitive load as an unvalidated usability risk and built a way to investigate it. I scoped the product question, designed the variants and event contract, implemented the workflow with AI assistance, and defined guardrails and next validation steps. No customer interviews or adoption gains are claimed.

chunks.pageTitle: Raasta: an instrumented product experiment · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: Two experiences, the same underlying rules
chunks.text:
Two experiences, the same underlying rules
The control displays the request, service, quantity and property-height fields together. Guided intake separates request and service selection, property details, and a review screen. Both use the same fictional price catalog and preserve the same human-review gate. This keeps the experiment focused on the intake experience.
The real GrowthBook JavaScript SDK assigns a stable anonymous alias to an arm using a pinned experiment key, equal weights and hash version 2. A missing identifier is not enrollment. The public demo lets a reviewer try either assigned experience.

chunks.pageTitle: Raasta: an instrumented product experiment · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: What success means
chunks.text:
What success means
The primary metric is the share of eligible exposed participants who reach a valid quote-review state. The funnel counts each participant once and ignores completion events before exposure. Reaching quote review is distinct from human approval, scheduling, revenue or a completed service job.
For planning only, a 40% baseline, a 15 percentage-point minimum detectable effect, two-sided 5% significance and 80% power imply about 173 participants per arm under a standard two-proportion approximation. A provisional target of 200 per arm adds planning headroom. These are assumptions to revisit after a pilot, not observed conversion results.

chunks.pageTitle: Raasta: an instrumented product experiment · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: Analytics with a narrow data contract
chunks.text:
Analytics with a narrow data contract
Recording begins only when the operator starts a local test session. Events identify exposure, intake start, reaching review, abandonment, validation errors and human decisions. The allowlist includes an anonymous alias, variation, a synthetic-data marker and optional elapsed milliseconds. It excludes request text, names, contact details and quote contents.
Events remain in browser memory until exported or explicitly sent for local verification. The actual PostHog Node SDK sends them to a temporary loopback collector. That collector independently checks delivery and payload contents. This verifies SDK transport; it does not constitute a deployed PostHog analytics backend.

chunks.pageTitle: Raasta: an instrumented product experiment · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: Guardrails before a winner
chunks.text:
Guardrails before a winner
Preserve identical quote logic and the human-review requirement.
Inspect validation errors, handoffs and time to review alongside completion.
Separate synthetic practice from consented usability-test data.
Agree eligibility, exclusions and a stopping rule before collecting randomized traffic.
Use initial usability sessions to find comprehension problems before attempting a powered experiment.

chunks.pageTitle: Raasta: an instrumented product experiment · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: What has actually been checked
chunks.text:
What has actually been checked
Actual GrowthBook bucketing is repeatable and exercises both arms.
Tests cover missing identity, duplicate completions and exposure ordering.
The actual PostHog SDK delivered all 300 events from a 100-participant synthetic simulation to the local collector.
Event validation strips unapproved properties.
The existing LangGraph approval/resume and idempotence checks remain in place.
These are implementation results. The simulation applies different outcome rules by design. Its conversion rates are authored examples, not evidence that guided intake improves a real product. No paid API, real customer traffic or business outcome was used to establish these checks.

chunks.pageTitle: Raasta: an instrumented product experiment · Ali Raza
chunks.heading: The next product decision
chunks.text:
The next product decision
Run consented usability sessions, inspect where participants hesitate, and revise the flow and instrumentation. Once traffic and baseline estimates are adequate, evaluate the predefined completion metric, uncertainty and guardrails at the planned horizon. The current evidence supports proceeding to that validation step.
